extract:
Whitesnake is an English hard rock band formed in 1978 by vocalist David Coverdale, shortly after the dissolution of Deep Purple, in which he had sung from 1973 to 1976. Rooted in the British blues-rock tradition before reinventing itself as a glossy, MTV-era arena act, the band has been active in various incarnations for more than four decades. It was based at first in England and later, as its commercial focus shifted, largely around Coverdale's life in the United States.

Coverdale's two solo albums, White Snake (1977) and Northwinds (1978), laid the groundwork. He then assembled a group that soon featured guitarists Micky Moody and Bernie Marsden, bassist Neil Murray, and keyboardist Jon Lord, his former Deep Purple bandmate. Drummer Ian Paice, also from Deep Purple, joined in 1979. The early sound drew on soul, R&B and the blues-rock of Free and Bad Company, steered by Coverdale's smoky baritone and producer Martin Birch.

The debut EP Snakebite and the album Trouble (1978) established the template. Lovehunter followed in 1979. Ready an' Willing (1980) delivered the band's first major hit, "Fool for Your Loving," and the live document Live... in the Heart of the City captured their stage strength. Come an' Get It (1981), featuring "Don't Break My Heart Again," and Saints & Sinners (1982), which contained the first version of "Here I Go Again," continued in this vein. After lineup upheaval, Slide It In (1984) brought in guitarist John Sykes and a heavier edge, and it was remixed for the American market. The commercial peak came with the 1987 self-titled album, released as 1987 in some territories. Co-written largely with Sykes and produced by Mike Stone and Keith Olsen, it featured re-recorded versions of "Here I Go Again" and "Crying in the Rain" alongside "Still of the Night" and "Is This Love." By the time of its release, Coverdale had replaced the recording band with Adrian Vandenberg, Vivian Campbell, Rudy Sarzo and Tommy Aldridge. Slip of the Tongue (1989) featured guitarist Steve Vai.

Label history spanned United Artists and EMI in Britain and Geffen Records in North America, with David Geffen's company driving the band's American breakthrough. The 1987 era placed Whitesnake firmly alongside glam metal contemporaries such as Bon Jovi and Def Leppard. Its videos featuring Tawny Kitaen, directed by Marty Callner, became MTV staples.

Critics in Britain often preferred the bluesier early records and regarded the later period as image-driven. Even so, the 1987 album sold in the multi-millions in the US, and "Here I Go Again" topped the Billboard Hot 100. The song has since become a fixture in films and advertising.

After a hiatus in the 1990s, punctuated by Restless Heart (1997), Coverdale revived Whitesnake in 2003 and released Good to Be Bad (2008), Forevermore (2011), The Purple Album (2015) and Flesh & Blood (2019), alongside extensive remastered and anniversary reissues of the classic catalog. In 2022 Coverdale wound down touring with a farewell tour, and he later announced his retirement. That move left the band's legacy as a bridge between 1970s British blues-rock and 1980s American arena metal.
title: Whitesnake
